findings.title: Audit log lacks principal identity — privileged actions cannot be tied to the requester (T-13 repudiation)
findings.description: _CorrelationIdMiddleware emits one INFO line per request carrying correlation_id/method/path but NOT the authenticated principal.key_id. A privileged action (DELETE /v1/tasks/{id} with scope=admin, GET /v1/metrics) leaves a log line from which the operator cannot recover WHO triggered the action — only the correlation_id that ties it to the wire response. T-13 declared: 'a privileged action cannot be tied to the request that caused it because response and log share no identifier'.
findings.code_snippet:
_audit_logger.info(
    "request correlation_id=%s method=%s path=%s",
    correlation_id, request.method, request.url.path,
)
findings.reasoning: Line 98-101 logs only correlation_id/method/path; the principal resolved later by require_scope (api/deps.py:77) is never persisted on request.state nor re-logged. An operator with the correlation_id can grep the audit log to find the request lifecycle, but cannot identify the caller — violates the FR-04 AC-4.2 'single chokepoint' contract and T-13's declared repudiation threat.
findings.suggested_fix: Store principal on request.state in require_scope (api/deps.py) AFTER verification, then in _CorrelationIdMiddleware.dispatch AFTER call_next, log the principal key_id alongside correlation_id (or via a second _audit_logger.info line).
findings.verify_evidence: Confirmed by independent trace: app.py:98-101 has no key_id reference; require_scope (api/deps.py:77) returns the Principal but does not store it on request.state; _CorrelationIdMiddleware (line 78) only sets request.state.correlation_id. No other audit log call captures the principal identity.

findings.title: v3 upgrade silently substitutes now() for missing/invalid finished_at — original timestamp lost (T-15 tampering)
findings.description: _now_or_default (line 82-92) returns datetime.now(tz=timezone.utc) whenever the payload's 'finished_at' is None OR fails fromisoformat parsing. The migration then writes this synthetic timestamp into task_results.finished_at. The original timestamp (which may have been absent in v1's free-form JSON blob) is lost; subsequent queries that order by finished_at (e.g. service/task_repo.list_results) get rows in arbitrary order based on migration wall-clock time.
findings.reasoning: Line 88-91: when 'finished_at' is missing (None) or malformed, the migration silently overwrites with the migration wall-clock time. v1's result_json was free-form, so many real-world entries will lack finished_at. Downgrade re-merges by task_id so the synthetic timestamps persist across the round-trip — original temporal order cannot be recovered. T-15 declared threat: 'the v3 result_json split loses or corrupts existing rows, and the downgrade cannot restore them'.
findings.suggested_fix: Use the parent Task row's created_at as a fallback (read tasks.created_at in the same SELECT), or skip the finished_at column (let server_default fill in), or raise so an operator notices the data gap. Avoid silent substitution.
findings.verify_evidence: Confirmed by independent trace: line 167 calls _now_or_default(entry.get('finished_at')) where entry may lack finished_at; line 178 does the same for legacy single-row payloads. _shared.json_loads_safe returns the parsed dict unchanged; there is no requirement on finished_at presence. The synthetic timestamp writes via task_results.insert() with finished_at = _now_or_default(...).

findings.title: _communicate_with_timeout does not kill subprocess on CancelledError — orphan survives outer cancellation (T-07 DoS)
findings.description: _communicate_with_timeout only handles asyncio.TimeoutError (its own internal timeout). When an outer cancellation propagates — e.g. drain() calls task.cancel() (runner.py:295), or run_with_timeout's asyncio.wait_for is cancelled — the asyncio.CancelledError bypasses the inner try/except, proc.kill() is never called, and the child process is orphaned. Repeated orphans consume the host (file descriptors, PIDs, memory).
findings.code_snippet:
try:
    stdout, stderr = await asyncio.wait_for(proc.communicate(), timeout=limit)
    return stdout, stderr, False
except asyncio.TimeoutError:
    proc.kill()
    stdout, stderr = await proc.communicate()
    return stdout, stderr, True
findings.reasoning: Lines 374-379: only asyncio.TimeoutError triggers proc.kill(). A BaseException-derived CancelledError (asyncio.CancelledError is a BaseException in Python 3.8+) raised by the outer asyncio.wait_for in run_with_timeout (line 334) or by drain (line 295) propagates past this try/except without killing proc. T-07 declared: 'runaway task ignores its deadline and leaves orphan processes that consume the host after the request ends'.
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap the inner wait_for in try/except (asyncio.TimeoutError, asyncio.CancelledError, BaseException) and always call proc.kill() before re-raising; or use asyncio.shield around proc.communicate() with an explicit cancel + kill pattern in a finally block.
findings.verify_evidence: Confirmed by independent trace: line 374 awaits asyncio.wait_for(proc.communicate(), timeout=limit); line 376-379 only catches TimeoutError. asyncio.CancelledError inherits from BaseException (Python 3.8+) so it bypasses this handler. drain() at line 295 calls t.cancel() on submitted tasks; run_with_timeout at line 334 awaits asyncio.wait_for(coro, ...) which cancels its wrapped task on its own timeout — in both paths proc.kill() is unreachable.

findings.title: ValidationProblem.detail carries Pydantic error.input — caller-supplied values echoed in 422 body (T-10 info disclosure)
findings.description: app.py:159 builds the ValidationProblem with detail=str(exc.errors()). Pydantic v2's errors() includes an 'input' field for every validation failure that echoes the rejected value verbatim. An attacker POSTing {"command": "sk-aBcDeFgHiJkLmN1234567890"} to /v1/tasks receives a 422 body containing the rejected plaintext secret (the 'input' field of the Pydantic error). Combined with any downstream log/observability tool that records 4xx bodies, the secret leaks.
findings.reasoning: Line 159 passes exc.errors() (list of dicts, JSON-serialisable) directly as detail. Each dict carries type/loc/msg/input/ctx; 'input' is the raw value. T-10 declared: 'unexpected exception returns a stack trace, SQL statement, schema name or filesystem path to the caller'. While no stack trace leaks, a caller-controlled value DOES leak through 'input', which combined with the secret-redaction regex (errors.py:22) NOT matching it (the value is opaque data, not a recognised secret pattern), means a bearer token posted in a wrong field gets echoed.
findings.suggested_fix: Strip the 'input' field from each error dict before stringifying; or build a custom safe-detail message that omits input/ctx and keeps only type/loc/msg.
findings.verify_evidence: Confirmed by independent trace: Pydantic v2 ValidationError.errors(include_url=False, include_input=True) (default) includes 'input' key with the rejected value verbatim. The string repr of the list is assigned to ValidationProblem.detail (errors.py:56-62). _problem_response (app.py:54-75) writes the body via problem_body which includes 'detail'. redact_secrets is NOT applied to the detail path. T-10 mitigations are partial.

findings.title: X-Correlation-Id header size not capped by middleware
findings.description: _CorrelationIdMiddleware accepts any-length X-Correlation-Id header value and stores it on request.state + emits it on the response. While Starlette caps the underlying header parse at ~64KB, the value flows into _audit_logger.info without a length limit, so a hostile caller can balloon log lines.
findings.code_snippet:
async def dispatch(self, request, call_next):
    correlation_id = (
        request.headers.get("X-Correlation-Id") or new_correlation_id()
    )
findings.reasoning: Line 95 reads the inbound header without bounding it. Starlette's default header size cap (around 64KB) limits the worst-case, so the exposure is bounded. Marked LOW for record-keeping; not exploitable in practice.
findings.suggested_fix: Cap correlation_id length (e.g. 128 chars) and fall back to new_correlation_id() if exceeded.
findings.verify_evidence: Refuted: Starlette/uvicorn default header cap is 65537 bytes (uvicorn.h11_max_incomplete_event_size default). An attacker cannot exceed that. Severity demoted to LOW; record-only.

resolution.refute_evidence: Starlette's default header parser caps each header value at the configured max-incomplete-event-size (uvicorn default 64KB). The exposure is bounded by the framework, not the middleware. No exploitable DoS in default config.

findings.title: Permissive CORS — T-04 refuted
findings.description: Threat T-04 declares 'hostile origin reads authenticated responses from a victim browser via permissive CORS'. The application mounts no CORS middleware; FastAPI/Starlette do not add CORS by default.
findings.reasoning: No CORSMiddleware is mounted. Without an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header, browsers block cross-origin reads of the response. The Settings.cors_origins field is defined but never read by any code path — config gap, not a vulnerability.
findings.suggested_fix: No fix needed. Optionally consume Settings.cors_origins to mount CORSMiddleware with an explicit allowlist when cross-origin is in scope.
findings.verify_evidence: Refuted: app.py:133-191 (create_app) mounts only _CorrelationIdMiddleware. grep 'CORSMiddleware|add_middleware' across src/ returns only the one line. No Access-Control-* headers are emitted. T-04 mitigation is the default deny.

resolution.refute_evidence: No CORSMiddleware mounted; FastAPI default is no CORS headers → browsers block cross-origin response reads. T-04 not exploitable in current config.

findings.title: String-built SQL — T-08 refuted
findings.description: Threat T-08 declares 'attacker-controlled status, cursor or name value alters query semantics through string-built SQL'.
findings.code_snippet:
query = (
    select(Task)
    .options(selectinload(Task.results))
    .order_by(Task.created_at.desc(), Task.id.desc())
    .limit(_MAX_LISTABLE)
)
if status is not None:
    query = query.where(Task.status == status)
findings.reasoning: All queries use SQLAlchemy ORM bound parameters (.where(Task.status == status) renders as a parameterised predicate). The cursor (line 474-485) is decoded via base64 + fromisoformat with explicit exception handling. No f-string / % / + concatenation into SQL.
findings.verify_evidence: Refuted: every .where() in task_repo.py uses bound parameters; the cursor path catches (binascii.Error, ValueError, UnicodeDecodeError) and returns ([], None). No raw SQL string interpolation anywhere.

resolution.refute_evidence: All SQL via SQLAlchemy ORM .where() bound-parameter form; no string-built SQL anywhere in task_repo.py. T-08 not exploitable.
